papers.title: Statistical approaches in ambispective cohort studies: Challenges and methodological insights.
papers.one_line: A structured review of ambispective cohort designs catalogs selection, lead-time, recall and time-varying confounding problems and answers each with a named technique, without supplying any criterion for when a retrospective and a prospective phase can be analyzed as one cohort.
papers.what_was_done: Statistical practice for cohorts that combine a retrospective phase built from hospital records, administrative databases and patient interviews with a prospective follow-up phase was reviewed from PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science, with thematic synthesis of the design-related challenges and the methods offered against them. Selection bias is attributed to hospital-record sampling that overrepresents severely ill patients and to loss to follow-up in the prospective phase, and is answered with propensity score matching and inverse probability weighting. Lead-time bias from historical screening protocols is answered with time-dependent Cox models, landmark analysis aligning patients at a standardized point after diagnosis, and joint modeling of longitudinal biomarkers with time-to-event outcomes. Recall bias in the retrospective phase, where exposure and adherence come from patient memory while the prospective phase has real-time documentation, is answered with validation against medical records, sensitivity analysis and probabilistic bias analysis. Time-varying confounders that are also intermediates are answered with time-dependent Cox models, marginal structural models and mixed-effects models. Missing data is answered with multiple imputation by chained equations, informative censoring with competing risk models and dropout-probability weights. No quantitative results, no worked example and no threshold for data comparability across the two phases are provided.

problems.evidence: The retrospective phase draws on hospital records, administrative databases and patient interviews while the prospective phase uses structured real-time collection, and the requirement stated is that definitions be uniform across the two. No procedure is given for verifying that a variable recorded from a chart in 2015 and the same variable collected prospectively in 2024 carry the same meaning, so harmonization remains an instruction rather than a check.
problems.quote: Study design and data collection should ensure uniform definitions and consistent data capture across retrospective and prospective periods

problems.evidence: Exposure and adherence in the retrospective phase are acknowledged to rest on patient memory, giving differential accuracy between the two phases of the same cohort. Validation against medical records is recommended only when self-reported data are unavoidable, so the default is that a measured variable enters the analysis with its error unquantified and identical treatment to a prospectively documented one.
problems.quote: When self-reported data are unavoidable, validation against medical records is recommended to improve data reliability.

problems.evidence: Dropout in the prospective phase is treated as a censoring nuisance to be reweighted by dropout probability or absorbed into a competing risk model, and gaps in the retrospective phase are treated as values to be imputed. The reasons a patient stops appearing in the record, which in this design include consent withdrawal, transfer of care and death, are never modeled as part of the causal structure that generates exposure and outcome.
problems.quote: Informative censoring due to nonrandom dropout in the prospective phase can bias survival estimates; solutions include competing risk models and IPW based on dropout probabilities

problems.evidence: Landmark analysis is offered as the fix for lead-time bias arising from different diagnostic timelines in the retrospective and prospective components, and the landmark is described only as a standardized time point after diagnosis. No rule fixes that point, and nothing prevents it from being chosen after survival curves have been inspected, in a design where the retrospective outcomes are already known at the time of analysis.
problems.quote: Landmark analysis has also been employed to align patients at a standardized time point postdiagnosis, ensuring comparability of survival estimates.

problems.evidence: Every challenge in the review is paired with a technique and none with a stopping rule: the closing prescription is a robust statistical analysis plan, interdisciplinary collaboration and methodological rigor. A design in which historical records are known to have missing laboratory results, incomplete treatment histories and documentation gaps is declared workable on the strength of planning rather than on any measured property of the data.
problems.quote: This review highlights the importance of a robust statistical analysis plan, interdisciplinary collaboration, and methodological rigor.

papers.title: Statistical Methods to Adjust for Treatment Switching in Real-World Clinical Studies: A Scoping Review and Descriptive Comparison.
papers.one_line: A scoping review of 45 methodological studies comparing treatment switching adjustments finds four families of methods, no ranking among them, and not one study that combined a switching adjustment with a missing data method.
papers.what_was_done: MEDLINE and Embase were searched to December 2024 for studies comparing at least two statistical methods for adjusting for treatment switching in real-world data; 2,474 records were screened, 80 went to full text, 20 were included from the database search and 25 more were added by reference checking and snowball search, giving 45 studies. Four families were identified: traditional analyses (intention to treat, per protocol, as treated, repeated measures), propensity score based methods (adjustment, time-varying matching, marginal structural models, sequential Cox), other g-methods (g-computation, structural nested models, longitudinal targeted maximum likelihood estimation) and methods that relax no unmeasured confounding (regression calibration, instrumental variables). A method-by-assumption grid was produced in which each row is a method and each column an assumption it relies on. No method emerged as preferred: the conclusion is that the choice depends on context, data and assumption plausibility. Several concrete gaps are quantified or stated: none of the 45 studies combined a switching adjustment with multiple imputation or another missing data method; over two-thirds of instrumental variable studies in prior reviews failed to fully address the assumptions required for a valid instrument; longitudinal targeted maximum likelihood has mainly been evaluated with a single-point exposure; and many of the methods are not implemented in commonly used software. Because several included studies used empirical rather than simulated data, no true effect was available against which their estimates could be scored.

future_research.gap: Combining treatment switching adjustment with missing data methods has never been evaluated
future_research.quote: However, none combined treatment switching adjustment methods with other methods to handle missing data, such as multiple imputation.

future_research.gap: Doubly robust methods are untested in complex longitudinal switching settings
future_research.quote: Future research should assess whether doubly robust methods consistently outperform other approaches in complex datasets with frequent switching and varying levels of missing data, ensuring accurate effect estimation in RWD studies.

problems.evidence: Forty-five studies comparing at least two adjustment methods produce no ordering: the closing recommendation is that the choice be guided by context, data and assumption plausibility. Worse for accountability, a share of those 45 are empirical analyses in which no true effect exists, so the comparison they report cannot say whether the choice of method changed the answer in the direction of truth.
problems.quote: Hence, all of these methods have strengths and limitations, and the choice should be guided by the study context, the nature of the data, and the plausibility of the underlying assumptions.

problems.evidence: A method-by-assumption grid is supplied in which each row is one of the identified methods and each column an assumption that must hold, with the consequence of violation stated. That is an assumption inventory at the level of the method. It stops short of the study level: the grid does not separate assumptions that a given dataset can diagnose from those it cannot, and it attaches no evidence from any particular emulation.
problems.quote: Each row represents a statistical method, and each column lists an assumption that must be met for the method to produce valid results.

problems.evidence: Only two of the four method families relax no unmeasured confounding, and both are gated on external information: regression calibration needs a representative validation sample and instrumental variables need a valid instrument. Prior reviews cited here found more than two-thirds of instrumental variable studies failed to address the required assumptions, so the workflow contains a slot for external validation evidence that is routinely left empty.
problems.quote: However, the practical application of these methods hinges on the availability of a representative validation sample or a valid IV, which can be highly challenging to identify.

problems.evidence: Intention to treat appeared in only three of the 45 studies and then mostly as a comparator, and its stated failure mode is that the effects of subsequent treatments are attributed to the original assignment. In real-world data where switching is driven by evolving prognosis, that attribution grows with follow-up, so the observational analogue of the intention to treat contrast degrades as the arms converge.
problems.quote: As a result, the effects of subsequent treatments are attributed to the original treatment, potentially introducing bias and misrepresenting the true effectiveness of the treatment under study.
problems.locator: Intention-to-treat analysis, assumptions, strengths, and limitations

problems.evidence: Inverse probability of censoring weights were the standard response to informative dropout across the included studies, and missingness was otherwise left untreated: none of the 45 combined a switching adjustment with multiple imputation. Real-world data with switching are characterized here as also having incomplete and inconsistently timed covariate measurement, so the observation process is being handled as a weighting nuisance rather than modeled.
problems.quote: This involves not only measuring all potential (time‐varying) confounders, but also ensuring that these measurements are performed consistently over time and not too long before treatment switching can occur.

problems.evidence: The stated barrier to adoption is that the identified methods are not available in commonly used statistical packages, and the remedy proposed is that future work publish tutorials with ready-to-use code. A field in which the analytic machinery itself is not distributed as runnable code is not one in which individual studies are distributing their weight diagnostics or phenotype logic.
problems.quote: Finally, many of the identified methods remain challenging to implement in practice, as they are not readily available in commonly used statistical software packages (e.g., SPSS, STATA).

papers.title: Statistical Methods for Baseline Adjustment and Cohort Analysis in Korean National Health Insurance Claims Data: A Review of PSM, IPTW, and Survival Analysis With Future Directions.
papers.one_line: A methods review of Korean National Health Insurance claims research reports that among 678 studies using customized datasets 56.93 percent were retrospective cohorts, and identifies washout period definition, diagnosis code validity and extreme weights as the recurring analytic weak points.
papers.what_was_done: Design and analysis practice for causal questions in Korean National Health Insurance Service claims data was reviewed, covering propensity score matching, inverse probability of treatment weighting, Cox proportional hazards models and the newer doubly robust, machine learning and marginal structural model approaches. Among 678 studies using customized NHIS datasets, retrospective cohort designs accounted for 56.93 percent, incidence and prevalence studies 15.34 percent, exposure-matched cohorts 12.68 percent, cross-sectional studies 8.26 percent, and nested case-control, case-control, case-crossover and cohort profile designs 2.95, 1.47, 0.88 and 0.88 percent; the ten most studied conditions together covered only 11.00 percent of the corpus. Claims records are described as an administrative byproduct with no predefined index time, so a washout period is required to fix study initiation, and diagnosis codes alone are stated not to identify disease without accompanying procedure codes. Recurring biases named are selection, immortal time, length-time, visit and misclassification bias. Weighting is described as unstable when propensity scores approach 0 or 1, with stabilization the recommended fix, and target trial emulation is listed as one of the designs that emerged during the COVID-19 period. No quantitative synthesis of bias magnitudes, no validation statistics for any code definition and no thresholds for adequacy are given.

future_research.gap: Integration of high-dimensional linked datasets with claims data lacks established analytic methods
future_research.quote: As more datasets become integrated with health insurance claims data, high-dimensional data analysis techniques will become essential, driving the development of more sophisticated research methodologies.

problems.evidence: Disease status in this data source is stated to require procedure codes alongside diagnosis codes before it can be treated as accurate, and misclassification bias is listed among the standard biases of claims research. Every design reviewed then carries that status forward as a binary eligibility, exposure or outcome variable, with no sensitivity analysis or validation statistic attached anywhere in the review.
problems.quote: Additionally, diagnosis codes alone do not provide direct information on treatment outcomes, necessitating the integration of procedure codes to accurately define diseases.
problems.locator: Characteristics and utilization of Korean health insurance claims data

problems.evidence: Positivity enters the review only as the observation that propensity scores near 0 or 1 generate extreme weights and estimation instability, and the remedy offered is stabilization of the weights. No step identifies which patients or which covariate patterns generated those scores, so the diagnostic and the fix both operate on the weight distribution rather than on the region of unsupported histories.
problems.quote: However, if the PSs are too close to 0 or 1, extremely large weights can be generated, which can lead to estimation instability.

problems.evidence: Claims data carry no clinical index date, so a washout period must be imposed to create one, and the review states this requirement without specifying a length, a rule for choosing it, or any protection against choosing it after inspecting outcomes. That decision fixes time zero for every subsequent eligibility and follow-up definition in the 678 studies described.
problems.quote: Consequently, a designated washout period is necessary to establish a clear study initiation point.

problems.evidence: Visit bias is listed among the standard biases of this data source, and reimbursement policy is described as directly altering whether patients continue to appear in the records. Cohorts assembled from encounter and prescription records therefore condition on a healthcare-use process that responds to policy rather than to health, which is a selection mechanism operating at eligibility.
problems.quote: Changes in government reimbursement policies can impact patient behavior; for instance, some patients who previously visited hospitals regularly may discontinue care when financial support is reduced.
problems.locator: Characteristics and utilization of Korean health insurance claims data

problems.evidence: The stated reason that a decade of NHIS sample cohort research fell short of expectations is limited understanding of the data characteristics and failure to account for the limits of big data. The prescription that follows is comprehension of the data structure and careful method selection, which is narrative guidance with no measurable criterion that would prevent a question from being asked of this source.
problems.quote: This discrepancy arose primarily due to a limited understanding of the characteristics of claims data and a failure to account for the inherent limitations of big data.

papers.title: Inference procedures in sequential trial emulation with survival outcomes: Comparing confidence intervals based on the sandwich variance estimator, bootstrap and jackknife.
papers.one_line: A simulation across 81 scenarios with 1000 datasets each shows that no single confidence interval method for the marginal risk difference in sequential trial emulation works across sample size, event rate and treatment prevalence; the recommendation flips between the linearised estimating function bootstrap and the sandwich variance estimator.
papers.what_was_done: Four confidence interval constructions for the counterfactual marginal risk difference under sequential trial emulation were compared: the simple sandwich variance estimator, the nonparametric bootstrap, two forms of a linearised estimating function bootstrap newly adapted to this setting, and two forms of jackknife resampling. Data were generated with treatment-confounder feedback, with baseline hazards set to give low (5 to 6.5 percent), medium (10 to 14 percent) and high (20 to 25 percent) event rates, and treatment prevalence tuned to 25 to 30, 50 to 60 and 75 to 80 percent, giving 81 scenarios at 1000 datasets each and 12 hours of compute on 67 cores. Nominal 95 percent coverage was rarely achieved at later trial visits when treatment prevalence was low or high, even at n = 5000, and absolute bias in the risk difference grew with visit number. The linearised estimating function bootstrap gave better coverage than the nonparametric bootstrap and the sandwich estimator at small to moderate sample sizes with low event rates, while the sandwich estimator was best and fastest at large sample sizes with medium to high event rates. Nonparametric bootstrap intervals took 2.4 to 4.5 times longer than sandwich intervals and the linearised version 1.8 to 3 times longer; the sandwich estimator produced construction failures from non-positive-definite variance matrices in the small-sample scenarios. Positivity was assessed only through summary statistics of the estimated weights by treatment arm. Dependent censoring was not included in the data-generating mechanism, no sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding was performed, and only pooled logistic models for the structural model were considered.

future_research.gap: Inference for sequential trial emulation under additive hazards models is undeveloped
future_research.quote: Inference procedures for STE based on additive hazard models warrant further research.

future_research.gap: No sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding exists for the sequential emulation setting
future_research.quote: In the specific setting of STE, sensitivity analysis methods for unmeasured confounding warrant further research.

future_research.gap: Inference after data-adaptive estimation of the weights is unresolved
future_research.quote: Because the consistency of the weighted estimators of the MSM parameters relies on correct specification of treatment and censoring models, data-adaptive methods are attractive.

problems.evidence: A linearised estimating function bootstrap is supplied and shown to be 1.6 times faster than the nonparametric bootstrap at n = 5000 while giving better coverage at small samples, so one scalable option now exists. It does not deliver a default: across 81 scenarios the best method changes with sample size, event rate and treatment prevalence, all methods lose nominal coverage at later visits under high treatment prevalence, and the sandwich estimator fails outright on non-positive-definite variance matrices in small samples.
problems.quote: For inference, the simple sandwich variance estimator is popular but conservative, while nonparametric bootstrap is computationally expensive, and a more efficient alternative, linearised estimating function (LEF) bootstrap, has not been adapted to STE.

problems.evidence: Coverage collapsed at later visits whenever treatment prevalence was 25 to 30 or 75 to 80 percent, and the positivity check offered was a table of estimated weight summary statistics stratified by assigned treatment. The conclusion drawn was that no practical positivity violation was present because weight estimation was stable, which is a statement about weights and not about which treatment histories had support.
problems.quote: This suggests that there was no practical violation of the positivity assumption manifested by the instability of the weight estimation.
problems.locator: Results, empirical bias and its impact on CI coverage

problems.evidence: Bias in the marginal risk difference increased with visit number in most scenarios even at n = 5000, and the stated cause was sparsity at later trial visits aggravated by treatment arm imbalance. The nominal sample size of the emulated cohort therefore says nothing about the information available in the sequences that actually identify the later-visit estimands.
problems.quote: This likely stemmed from data sparsity issues at later trial visits that were aggravated by treatment arm imbalance caused by low or high treatment prevalence.
problems.locator: Results, empirical bias and its impact on CI coverage

problems.evidence: The reported estimand is the counterfactual marginal risk difference over time rather than a hazard ratio, and the reason given is that the counterfactual hazard ratio lacks a causal interpretation. The step is incomplete: the risk difference is constructed from marginal structural model hazard ratio estimates combined with a baseline hazard estimate, so consistency still rests on the survival model being correctly specified.
problems.quote: The counterfactual hazard ratio has been criticised as lacking a causal interpretation, and it has been proposed that other estimands be used instead, for example, the marginal risk difference (MRD).

problems.evidence: Patients enter several emulated trials, which is why the simple sandwich variance estimator is conservative and why every resampling scheme must resample patients rather than trial rows. The efficiency gain of the expansion is thus paid for in inference: at low treatment prevalence, the regime the design is meant to serve, the intervals lose nominal coverage at later visits for every method compared.
problems.quote: Since STE is particularly useful for data scenarios with small numbers of patients initiating treatments at any given time (low treatment prevalence) and with low event rates, LEF bootstrap offers a useful alternative to the sandwich variance estimator and the nonparametric bootstrap for CI construction, especially in small/medium sample sizes.

problems.evidence: The entire simulation and the applied analysis proceed under an assumption of no unmeasured confounders, which is acknowledged as unlikely to hold in observational databases, and the only proposals named are instrumental variables and a general longitudinal sensitivity analysis for point or general settings. No negative control, proxy or validation-data step is part of the emulation workflow described.
problems.quote: Throughout this article, it was assumed that there were no unmeasured confounders.

papers.title: Research Advance of Causal Inference in Clinical Medicine: A Bibliometrics Analysis via Citespace.
papers.one_line: A CiteSpace analysis of 4,316 Web of Science records from 1986 to 2024 finds marginal structural models to have the highest keyword citation burst rate in medical causal inference, while naming treatment saturation and weight model misspecification as the unresolved limitations.
papers.what_was_done: A bibliometric map of causal inference in clinical medicine was built from 4,316 Web of Science Core Collection documents published between January 1986 and December 2024, using CiteSpace for co-authorship, co-citation and keyword co-occurrence networks. The United States contributed 2,452 publications, over 50 percent of the corpus; Harvard University led institutions with 203; the most cited authors were Robins with 1,148 citations and Rubin with 1,100, followed by Hernan with 977; the American Journal of Epidemiology was the most cited journal with 1,984 citations. Marginal structural models ranked first by keyword citation burst rate, with big data, DNA methylation, instruments and robust estimation identified as emerging fronts. The narrative synthesis identifies treatment saturation, where all observed subjects receive the same treatment in a given state, as a situation in which marginal structural models cannot estimate accurate causal effects, and cites evidence that inverse probability weighted marginal effects are highly sensitive to misspecification of the weight model, listing covariate balancing propensity scores, residual balancing and targeted maximum likelihood as competing remedies. No study-level quality appraisal, no estimand extraction and no assessment of assumption reporting were performed; coverage was limited to English-language records in a single database.

future_research.gap: Reporting frameworks for causal claims in observational studies are not settled
future_research.quote: Future research should continue to explore and refine these frameworks to enhance the quality and reliability of observational study outcomes.

problems.evidence: Treatment saturation is named as the situation in which a marginal structural model cannot learn potential outcomes under alternative treatments, which is exactly a region of covariate history without support. Nothing in the field map identifies a diagnostic that names those histories; the remedies listed are further modeling techniques, so a positivity failure is presented as a modeling problem.
problems.quote: In such scenarios, MSM may struggle to estimate accurate causal effects, as it cannot learn from the data the potential outcomes under different treatment conditions.

problems.evidence: Electronic health records are the dominant substrate for counterfactual analysis in the mapped literature, and the assessment of their fitness is a sentence stating that accuracy, completeness and consistency are critical. Across 4,316 records no threshold, no minimum completeness and no rule that would stop a study is reported.
problems.quote: While EHRs have received much attention from researchers, the accuracy, completeness, and consistency of the EHRs data itself are critical for effective counterfactual analysis.

problems.evidence: The forward-looking sections attach the improvement of causal inference to big data volume, random forests, support vector machines and deep neural networks for propensity score estimation. Confounding is not addressed by any of these; the expectation stated is that more computation will yield more detailed causal inference, which is a claim about estimation applied to an identification problem.
problems.quote: With the integration of big data and machine learning technologies, more detailed causal inference is expected to be realized in the future, providing real-time and precise support for clinical decision-making.

problems.evidence: Weight truncation, covariate balancing propensity scores, residual balancing, stabilized weights and targeted maximum likelihood are listed side by side as responses to the sensitivity of inverse probability weighting to weight model misspecification. No ordering, no default and no requirement that a study demonstrate its choice mattered emerges from a corpus of 4,316 records.
problems.quote: Previous studies have shown that the marginal effects of IPW estimation are highly sensitive to model misspecification in constructing the weights.

papers.title: Penalized G-estimation for effect modifier selection in a structural nested mean model for repeated outcomes.
papers.one_line: A doubly robust penalized G-estimator selects effect modifiers in a structural nested mean model for repeated outcomes, but when both the treatment and treatment-free models are misspecified it fails to select the true modifier in more than 70 percent of simulations.
papers.what_was_done: A penalized G-estimator with an oracle property was developed for a linear structural nested mean model with a proximal outcome measured at every occasion, selecting effect modifiers at the same time as it estimates the blip parameters. Simulations at n = 200 and n = 500 with 500 replications each compared independent, exchangeable and unstructured working correlation structures: exact selection of the true blip model exceeded 90 percent in most settings with error variance 1, fell when error variance rose to 4, and false negative and false positive rates were highest under working independence when outcomes were correlated. Double robustness was verified across four misspecification scenarios at n = 500 with J = 6 sessions; under joint misspecification of the treatment and treatment-free models the true modifier was dropped in more than 70 percent of replications, with bias toward the null. The application used an open cohort of 474 patients undergoing chronic hemodiafiltration at two facilities, 170,761 dialysis sessions in total, restricted to the first 6 consecutive post-dilution sessions, with the exposure defined as the facility. Under an AR1 working correlation, cancer status was selected as the sole modifier: mean convection volume was 1.85 L lower at the hospital site for patients without cancer and 2.04 L higher for patients with cancer. Informative censoring was not handled, no variable selection was performed for the treatment model, and identification of weak modifiers remained unsolved.

future_research.gap: Weak effect modifiers are not reliably identified by the selection procedure
future_research.quote: A challenge still remains in the identification of weak EMs, and this would be an interesting topic for future research.

future_research.gap: Informative censoring is not accommodated
future_research.quote: We also did not address informative censoring in this paper, but this is a possibility for a future extension.

problems.evidence: Double robustness is the flexibility on offer, and the simulation shows its boundary precisely: with a null propensity model and an omitted nonlinear term in the treatment-free model the true effect modifier was excluded in more than 70 percent of replications regardless of working correlation, with the bias driven toward the null. Adding estimation flexibility does not recover a modifier that misspecification has erased.
problems.quote: When both the treatment and the treatment-free models were incorrect (Scenario 4), the proposed method did not select the true EM, L (5) , in more than 70% of the simulations irrespective of what the corstr was.

problems.evidence: Data-adaptive selection produced a subgroup whose estimated effect reverses sign: 1.85 L lower convection volume at the hospital site for patients without cancer against 2.04 L higher for patients with cancer, in a cohort of 474 patients restricted to 6 sessions each. Cancer is a small stratum in a dialysis population and no overlap or positivity assessment is reported for the exposure within it, so the subgroup with the most extreme estimate is the one with the least support.
problems.quote: Under the AR1 corstr, cancer was selected by the method, indicating that the effect of dialysis facility on the convection volume differs by the cancer status of the patient.

problems.evidence: Selection is driven by a penalized estimating equation for the blip parameters themselves rather than by a prediction criterion, so the tuning target is the causal contrast and the oracle property is proved for it. The nuisance side is untouched: the propensity score was fitted by unpenalized logistic regression on all candidate confounders with no selection at all, and the acknowledgment is that such selection may be necessary in a high-dimensional setup.
problems.quote: Although we did not perform variable selection for the treatment model in our hemodiafiltration application, such selection may be necessary in practice, especially in a high-dimensional setup

problems.evidence: Outcomes are recorded at the end of each successful dialysis session, so the observation process is the treatment process, and sessions that did not take place are simply absent. The asymptotics are derived for a constant number of sessions per patient with unequal cluster sizes handled numerically, and censoring is left out entirely, so the mechanism generating the session sequence is never part of the causal model.
problems.quote: In this section, we study the asymptotic properties of the proposed penalized G-estimator, where we assume a constant cluster size (ie, the same number of sessions for patients).

problems.evidence: Four working correlation structures were fitted to the same hemodiafiltration data and three to the simulated data, and the choice changed both selection and precision: false negative and false positive rates under working independence exceeded those under exchangeable and unstructured structures. Nothing in the procedure requires reporting how the selected modifier set would change across those structures.
problems.quote: In this case, the FN and FP rates produced by the working independent structure are higher than the other 2 structures.

papers.title: An introduction to inverse probability weighting and marginal structural models: The case of environmental tobacco exposure and attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder behaviors.
papers.one_line: A didactic marginal structural model on 1053 children estimates a cumulative effect of tobacco exposure on first-grade ADHD behaviors of 0.27 with the two exposure periods collapsed into averages chosen for simplicity, and treats untestable ignorability as satisfied when the weights look well behaved.
papers.what_was_done: Inverse probability of treatment weighting and a marginal structural model were demonstrated on the Family Life Project, 1053 children, 51 percent male and 44 percent Black, with environmental tobacco exposure quantified by salivary cotinine assayed at the 6, 15, 24, 48 and 90 month home visits; logged cotinine ranged from -2.59 to 6.75 with across-time correlations of 0.62 to 0.77. The five occasions were collapsed into two developmental periods, infancy through toddlerhood at 6 to 24 months and early childhood at 48 to 90 months. Stabilized weights had standard deviation 1.53 for the single-exposure analysis and 1.7 for the final marginal structural weight, with a maximum weight of 21.53; models were rerun with weights coded at the 1st and 99th percentiles. Covariate balance was assessed by correlation with exposure, median 0.16 before weighting and 0.04 after, with four weighted correlations above the 0.1 threshold and a maximum of 0.125. For the single averaged exposure, unadjusted regression gave 0.31, covariate adjustment 0.21 and inverse probability weighting 0.25, all with p below 0.001. In the marginal structural model the infancy to toddlerhood effect was 0.14 with p = 0.03, the early childhood effect 0.13 with p = 0.07, and the cumulative effect 0.27 with p below 0.001. Propensity scores for the continuous exposure were estimated by linear regression.

future_research.gap: Balance across many treatment histories becomes unmanageable and no rule fixes the number of exposure periods
future_research.quote:
periods can become unwieldy to manage, and efforts to ensure balance across treatment
histories can become complicated.

future_research.gap: Propensity score estimation for continuous exposures is not settled
future_research.quote: Significant improvements in propensity score estimation for continuous treatment exposures include the use of generalized boosted models (GBM)

problems.evidence: Five cotinine measurements were averaged into two period-level exposures, so every distinct exposure history with the same period mean is treated as the same treatment. The stated reason is didactic simplicity, and the acknowledged consequence is that time-varying confounding may not be fully accounted for. Nothing clinical or biological defines the equivalence class, and the advice offered is to rely on theory.
problems.quote: First, for didactic reasons, the study simplified treatment exposures by averaging exposures experienced within developmental periods.

problems.evidence: The time grid is two windows carved out of five measurement occasions, and the number and duration of those windows fixes what the estimated period-specific effects of 0.14 and 0.13 mean. The only guidance given for that choice is theory, applied by the analyst after the data are in hand, with no outcome-blind procedure and no report of how the estimates move under an alternative grid.
problems.quote: Whenever possible, researchers should rely on theory when deciding on the number and durations of treatment histories.

problems.evidence: Ignorability is stated as untestable, and correct specification of the weight model is stated to be untestable directly but treatable as satisfied when the weights are well behaved and covariates balance. Both then feed the same reported estimates with no marker distinguishing them: a balance table stands in for a diagnosable assumption while the undiagnosable one is carried forward on a sentence.
problems.quote: This assumption is untestable and underscores the importance of measuring all the relevant variables that represent the selection mechanism that accounts for individual differences in differential treatment exposure.

problems.evidence: The maximum stabilized weight reached 21.53 against a mean near 1, and the response was to refit with weights coded at the 1st and 99th percentiles. That truncation changes the estimand without identifying which children generated the extreme weights or which exposure histories lacked support, so the diagnostic and the remedy both describe the weight distribution.
problems.quote: To test the effect of extreme weights on our results, we run the final models with weights that were bottom- and top-coded at the 1st and 99th percentile, respectively.

problems.evidence: Propensity scores for a continuous exposure were estimated by linear regression, and the justification recorded is ease of use and familiarity to the intended readership, with generalized boosted models and the covariate balancing generalized propensity score named afterwards as improvements not applied. No result is reported showing whether that choice moved the estimates of 0.14, 0.13 and 0.27.
problems.quote: This approach was used because of general ease of use and familiarity to developmental researchers.

problems.evidence: Unmeasured confounding is the only violated assumption given a sensitivity tool, and that tool is the E-value, a single number for a single unmeasured confounder. Measurement error in parent-reported ADHD, the averaging of exposure within periods and the linear propensity model are all live in the same analysis, and no device is offered that varies any of them jointly with confounding.
problems.quote: There are proposed sensitivity analyses which can be used to estimate the robustness of findings to potential unmeasured confounders, such as the E-value by VanderWeele and Ding (2017)

papers.title: Assessing Methods for Adjusting Estimates of Treatment Effectiveness for Patient Nonadherence in the Context of Time-to-Event Outcomes and Health Technology Assessment: A Simulation Study.
papers.one_line: Across 90 simulated scenarios with 1900 replications each, inverse probability of censoring weighting, structural nested failure time models and a simple per-protocol analysis all left about 20 to 26 percent average bias in the restricted mean survival difference under perfect adherence, and per protocol matched the g-methods.
papers.what_was_done: Trial datasets with a time-to-event outcome and simulated non-adherence were generated around a kidney transplant graft survival setting, with the estimand defined as the difference in restricted mean survival times in all patients had there been no non-adherence. Seven factors were varied, including the type of non-adherence (initiation, implementation, persistence), its level, sample size, the underlying hazard pattern, treatment effect size, the relationship between effect and adherence, and time-dependent treatment effect, giving 90 scenarios at 1900 simulations each. In implementation scenarios average percent bias was 20 percent for inverse probability of censoring weighting (range 7 to 37), 20 percent for the structural nested failure time model (8 to 38), 20 percent for per protocol (8 to 38) and 40 percent for intention to treat (20 to 75). In persistence scenarios the averages were 26, 26 and 26 percent for the three adjustments against 47 percent for intention to treat. Across the 34 initiation scenarios percent bias ranged from -29 to 110 for weighting, -34 to 108 for the structural nested model, -32 to 102 for per protocol and -18 to 200 for intention to treat. On the absolute scale the g-methods produced 0.019 years, about 7 days, against 0.020 for per protocol in implementation scenarios; the structural nested model gave 0.035 years overall in initiation scenarios and 0.015 years with large samples. Small sample sizes degraded the g-methods below per protocol in 5 of 18 persistence scenarios. Only three time points were simulated per dataset, and a cited review reported that 13 percent of trials account for adherence at all.

future_research.gap: Data-generating mechanisms realistic enough to separate g-methods from per protocol do not exist
future_research.quote: In order to examine this issue further, more complex DGMs may be required, and this could be an important area for future research.

future_research.gap: Cost as well as effectiveness must be adjusted to the expected adherence level and no method does this
future_research.quote: The focus of this simulation study was on the impact of non-adherence on treatment effectiveness, but in an HTA, costs would also need to be adjusted to reflect adherence levels expected in clinical practice.

problems.evidence: A per-protocol analysis, which makes no attempt to model time-dependent confounding, matched inverse probability of censoring weighting and the structural nested failure time model at 20 percent average bias in implementation scenarios and 26 percent in persistence scenarios, and beat them in 5 of 18 persistence scenarios with small samples. The complex estimator is therefore not defensible as a default on these numbers, and the direction of the gap depends on how strongly prognosis drives non-adherence.
problems.quote: Another important research finding relates to PP analysis, which in many scenarios had a similar level of performance to that of the g-methods.

problems.evidence: The adherence level the analysis adjusts to is a protocol component that cannot be observed, and the level chosen was perfect adherence because it was simple, while the quantity wanted for a health technology assessment is the effect at the adherence expected in routine care. The 90 scenarios therefore estimate a different, analysis-defined estimand rather than a noisy version of the decision-relevant one.
problems.quote: For simplicity, the level we chose to adjust to was perfect adherence, but in reality, we would adjust to the level of adherence expected in standard clinical practice.

problems.evidence: After the best available adjustment, average percent bias remained at 20 percent in implementation scenarios, 26 percent in persistence scenarios, and as high as 110 percent in individual initiation scenarios, in a study framed explicitly for health technology assessment. No threshold is available against which a submitted analysis carrying that residual bias could be judged adequate or inadequate.
problems.quote: The adjustment methods (IPCW, SNFTM, PP) all improve on this by reducing bias by about a half or more, even though with these better adjustment methods considerable bias may remain in some scenarios.

problems.evidence: Small sample size is identified as the factor that pushes the g-methods below the simple per-protocol comparison, and with only three time points per dataset the non-adherence process could not be modeled accurately. The methods that require time-varying confounder modeling are precisely the ones that fail when the effective information per time point is thin, which is the ordinary condition of an emulation after eligibility and weighting.
problems.quote: Small sample size has a negative impact on the performance of g-methods leading to higher bias compared to PP.

problems.evidence: The reported quantity is a difference in restricted mean survival times rather than a hazard ratio, and the counterfactual adherence condition defining it is stated up front, so estimand and effect measure are aligned. It does not close the entry: the population is all patients under an adherence condition nobody achieves, so the number that reaches a reimbursement decision still describes a regime that was never implementable.
problems.quote: In reality, achieving zero non-adherence is not possible in most clinical settings and instead we would expect adherence to be lower in standard clinical practice than in RCTs

problems.evidence: Intention to treat was the worst method in every non-adherence type, reaching 200 percent bias in initiation scenarios, and its bias grew with the size of the true treatment effect. As adherence in the two arms converges the assigned-treatment contrast measures less of the effect it names, so the attenuation is a property of the design and not a small-sample artifact.
problems.quote: ITT bias was amplified by a larger treatment effect size.

papers.title: How estimating nuisance parameters can reduce the variance (with consistent variance estimation).
papers.one_line: A consistent sandwich variance estimator is derived for inverse probability weighting, marginal structural models and structural nested models when the nuisance parameters are also estimated, replacing a bootstrap that took over 8 hours on a cluster with a calculation that takes seconds.
papers.what_was_done: General variance theory was developed for estimators solving unbiased estimating equations that involve a finite-dimensional nuisance parameter estimated in a first step, covering inverse probability of treatment weighting, marginal structural models and structural nested models. Four further results hold when the nuisance parameter solves partial score equations and the parameter of interest does not depend on it: the true limiting variance is smaller or unchanged when the nuisance is estimated rather than known; the sandwich estimator that ignores nuisance estimation is conservative; a consistent correction is available; and if the estimator with the true nuisance plugged in is efficient the correction is zero. Simulations with 8000 datasets showed the conservative estimator producing confidence intervals up to 27 percent wider than needed with over-coverage of 96.0 to 98.6 percent in one scenario, against 0.6 to 1.8 percent excess width and 95.0 to 95.6 percent coverage for the corrected estimator. At a sample size of 130, mirroring the applied analysis, 6.3 percent of datasets returned a negative consistent variance estimate; at 1000 none did. The applications were an inverse probability weighted comparison of ceftazidime-avibactam against colistin in 38 and 99 patients with resistant bacterial infections, where the original analysis used a semiparametric bootstrap, and a time-dependent structural nested mean model for antiretroviral initiation timing whose nonparametric bootstrap took more than 8 hours on a large computing cluster. The theory does not cover nuisance parameters fitted by super learner or other methods that are not unbiased estimating equations.

future_research.gap: Small-sample corrections for sandwich variances in the presence of nuisance parameters are undeveloped
future_research.quote: Developing such methods in settings with nuisance parameters, probably depending on the forms of U1 and U2, is an interesting topic for future research.

problems.evidence: A closed-form consistent sandwich variance is supplied for exactly the estimators an emulation uses, and the payoff is measured: a structural nested mean model application whose nonparametric bootstrap needed over 8 hours on a computing cluster is served by a sandwich calculation on a laptop, and the conservative alternative gave intervals up to 27 percent too wide. It is not yet a default: 6.3 percent of datasets at n = 130 returned a negative variance estimate, and the result requires the nuisance parameters to solve score equations.
problems.quote: The importance of the theory in this article is best illustrated in the application of Web-appendix D, where the nonparametric bootstrap took more than 8 hours on a large computing cluster; the sandwich estimator took very little time on a laptop.

problems.evidence: Two variance estimators for the same weighted estimate differ by up to 27 percent in interval width, with over-coverage of 96.0 to 98.6 percent from the conservative one against 95.0 to 95.6 percent from the corrected one across 8000 datasets. Nothing requires a study reporting an inverse probability weighted contrast to state which it used or to show that the difference did not change its conclusion.
problems.quote: In the second simulation scenario, it is very beneficial to use the consistent estimator for the variance developed in this article, with the conservative estimator of the variance leading to confidence intervals up to 27% wider than needed and substantial over-coverage

problems.evidence: The motivating applied comparison rests on 38 patients treated with the new antibiotic against 99 on the comparator, and at the matching simulated sample size of 130 the consistent variance estimator returned a negative value in 6.3 percent of datasets. The asymptotic machinery that licenses the interval breaks down at the sample sizes that survive real eligibility and comparator restriction.
problems.quote: In the simulations of IPTW with a sample size of 130 (Section 6 Table 3), which mirror the bacterial infections application of Section 5, 6.3% of the datasets resulted in negative consistent estimates of the variance.

problems.evidence: The variance theory holds when the nuisance models are correctly specified and estimated by unbiased estimating equations; when a nuisance model is misspecified the sandwich estimator need not even be conservative, and the parameter of interest may not be identified at all. Targeted estimators fitted with super learner fall outside the coverage of the result, so the flexible fit that is supposed to reduce misspecification is the case in which the inference is unsupported.
problems.quote: The sandwich estimator for the variance of ψ̂ does not need to be conservative if the nuisance parameter model is misspecified. In such settings the parameter of interest ψ may not even be identified.

papers.title: Change in employment status and its causal effect on suicidal ideation and depressive symptoms: A marginal structural model with machine learning algorithms.
papers.one_line: A marginal structural model weighted by a random forest propensity score, selected because it had the highest area under the curve at 0.702, estimates an odds ratio of 2.07 for suicidal ideation after a move from standard to non-standard employment.
papers.what_was_done: Waves 8 to 15 of the Korean Welfare Panel Study, 2013 to 2020, supplied 13,294 observations from 3,621 participants who held standard employment at baseline, classified at follow-up as maintaining standard employment or having moved to non-standard employment. Eight machine learning algorithms were fitted to predict the exposure and the one with the largest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was retained; random forest won at 0.702 with 95 percent confidence interval 0.686 to 0.718, with standard logistic regression close behind. Stabilized inverse probability weights from that model were used in a marginal structural model with a random intercept, giving an odds ratio of 2.07 with 95 percent confidence interval 1.16 to 3.70 for suicidal ideation, attenuating to 1.97 with interval 1.11 to 3.48 after further baseline adjustment, and a coefficient of 0.37 with interval 0.19 to 0.55 for depressive symptoms in the doubly robust model. Balance was reported as a standardized mean difference below 0.1 for all covariates in the pseudo-population, although some covariates including home ownership and urban residence were worse balanced after weighting than before. Twenty-four variables entered the weight model. Employment change and past-year suicidal ideation were measured in the same survey wave, the reasons for employment change were not recorded, and district-level employment rate was not available.

future_research.gap: Voluntary and involuntary transitions to non-standard employment are not distinguished
future_research.quote:
Therefore, future studies
should consider the reasons of change in employment status.

problems.evidence: Eight candidate weight models were compared on a single criterion, cross-validated area under the curve, and the winner scored 0.702 against a logistic regression that performed almost as well. Discrimination of the exposure model is a prediction property; no criterion tied to bias in the odds ratio of 2.07 or to the variance of the weights entered the selection, so the nuisance model was tuned for the wrong objective.
problems.quote:
We selected the algorithm with
the largest AUC as that which performed best.

problems.evidence: Eight algorithms, 24 covariates and a doubly robust outcome model were deployed, and the residual confounding acknowledged afterwards is structural rather than statistical: district employment rate was never measured. The estimated odds ratio of 2.07 is presented as causal on the strength of the flexible weight model, but flexibility cannot supply a variable the panel does not contain.
problems.quote:
So we cannot completely rule out the possibility of
violating exchangeability assumptions for our estimates from MSM
interpreted as casual.

problems.evidence: The exposure is a change in employment status observed between two survey waves, not an intervention anyone assigns, so there is no treatment version, no assignment unit and no time at which a policy could act. The estimate of 2.07 nonetheless carries a causal label, and the acknowledged inability to distinguish a layoff from a voluntary move shows the exposure bundles interventions with opposite expected effects.
problems.quote:
Fourth, we did not consider reasons for changes in employment
status.

problems.evidence: Everything coded as a move to non-standard employment is treated as one treatment, yet the cited evidence is that people who changed voluntarily reported higher life satisfaction. Two versions with opposite expected effects on the outcome sit inside one exposure category, and no procedure in the analysis separates them or bounds the resulting contrast.
problems.quote:
Cuyper & Witte ( 35 )reported that people who voluntarily changed their
employment status from standard to non-standard were more likely to
report a higher level of life satisfaction.

problems.evidence: Exposure and outcome share a survey wave and the outcome window looks back twelve months, so ideation could precede the employment change it is attributed to. The time grid is inherited from the panel's annual waves with no separation interval imposed, and the acknowledged consequence is that the suicidal ideation estimate of 2.07 may be reversed in direction.
problems.quote:
First, we could not
be free from the possibility of reverse causality, especially in the
analysis of suicidal ideation, because change in employment status and
suicidal ideation over the past year were measured in the same wave of
survey.

problems.evidence: Support for the exposure contrast is reported as a standardized mean difference below 0.1 for all covariates in the pseudo-population, with home ownership and urban residence noted as worse balanced after weighting than before. Balance of means is not support: no weight distribution, no truncation rule and no identification of which worker histories had negligible probability of either employment path is given.
problems.quote:
It was observed that the standardized mean
difference was higher in the pseudo-population than in the raw
population for some covariates, including house owner, and urban area.

papers.title: History-restricted marginal structural model and latent class growth analysis of treatment trajectories for a time-dependent outcome.
papers.one_line: A history-restricted marginal structural model over latent adherence trajectory groups applied to 57,211 statin initiators gives a relative risk of 0.65 with interval 0.57 to 0.75 under g-computation but 0.77 with interval 0.53 to 1.10 under inverse probability weighting, an opposite conclusion from the same data.
papers.what_was_done: Latent class growth analysis was combined with a nonparametric history-restricted marginal structural model so that treatment trajectory groups can change from one time window to the next and the outcome can occur during follow-up. Because hazard ratios carry built-in selection bias and no survival curve can be assembled when the trajectory group changes across windows, the causal parameter chosen was the absolute risk in each interval, fitted with weighted log-binomial and Poisson working models. Three estimators were compared: unstabilized inverse probability weighting, g-computation and a pooled longitudinal targeted maximum likelihood estimator with and without SuperLearner, with a variance correction for dependence between influence functions across windows. Simulations used 1,000 datasets of size 5,000 with one, two and three windows of size 3 and three trajectory groups; g-computation and pooled targeted maximum likelihood were unbiased, inverse probability weighting was slightly more biased with larger standard errors, and coverage ran 94 to 100 percent for the targeted estimator, 90 to 100 percent for weighting and 89 to 92 percent for g-computation with one window. The application used the Quebec integrated chronic disease surveillance system: 57,211 statin initiators aged over 65 with no cardiovascular history, followed 60 months, with the first interval containing all 57,211 and the last only 2,315 still alive and event free. Mean adherence across windows was 0.99, 0.54 and 0.02 in the three groups. Against the lowest adherence group the highest adherence group gave relative risks of 0.77 with interval 0.53 to 1.10 by weighting, 0.65 with interval 0.57 to 0.75 by g-computation and 0.75 with interval 0.59 to 0.97 by the targeted estimator; the middle adherence group gave 1.07 by weighting and 0.81 by g-computation, all intervals covering 1.

future_research.gap: Missingness in treatment trajectories is assumed to be at random conditional on the groups and relaxations are undeveloped
future_research.quote: Nonetheless, extensions that relax the assumptions on the missingness mechanism for the LCGA step may be an interesting direction for future work.

future_research.gap: No procedure selects the window size or the number of trajectory groups
future_research.quote: In practice, a user can encounter challenges regarding the choice of the hyperparameters s which is the size of a time interval or J the number of trajectory groups.

problems.evidence: Three estimators were run on the same 57,211 statin initiators under the same working model and returned different conclusions: weighting gave 0.77 with interval 0.53 to 1.10, compatible with harm up to a relative risk of 1.10, while g-computation gave 0.65 with interval 0.57 to 0.75, excluding the null. The choice of estimator, not the data, decides whether high statin adherence is reported as beneficial.
problems.quote: However, the IPW gave a slightly different, more inconclusive, result.

problems.evidence: The cohort begins with 57,211 individuals in the first time interval and ends with 2,315 still alive and free of cardiovascular events in the last, a loss of 96 percent of the sample before the final interval contributes. The estimand is defined across all intervals, so the later windows that carry the long-term adherence contrast rest on a fraction of the headline database size.
problems.quote: The first time interval was composed by 57,211 statin initiators and the last interval by 2,315 individuals who were still alive and CVD-free.

problems.evidence: Latent class growth analysis reduces thousands of observed adherence patterns to three groups with mean adherence 0.99, 0.54 and 0.02, and the estimand is then defined conditional on the groups that were formed, which makes the equivalence classes explicit rather than implicit. It does not close the entry: the groups are stated to be points of support rather than a true data-generating structure, the number of groups is a hyperparameter chosen by information criteria, and no clinical criterion establishes that adherence 0.54 is one treatment.
problems.quote: As argued in Nagin [ 11 ] and Diop et al. [ 10 ], trajectory groups are not meant to represent the true data-generating distribution but can be seen as points of support.

problems.evidence: The window size fixes what a trajectory group means and therefore what the absolute risk contrast estimates, and the acknowledged failure mode of a wrong choice is a window in which everyone is exposed or nobody is. The check offered is to inspect the data distribution across intervals, which is not an outcome-blind selection rule, and no report shows how the relative risks of 0.65 and 0.77 move under a different window size.
problems.quote: With the wrong choice of s , estimation problems might arise.

problems.evidence: A variance correction for the dependence between influence functions across overlapping windows was derived for the pooled targeted estimator and validated against block bootstrapping, which supplies one scalable route where the naive influence function calculation does not apply. It does not become a default: the simple option named for the weighted estimating-equation fit is a sandwich estimator that treats the weights as known and is conservative, and g-computation still needed 50 bootstrap replications in simulation and 100 in the application.
problems.quote: A simple practical solution for inference is to use the sandwich variance estimator of the GEE routine, which treats the weights as known and results in conservative statistical inferences

problems.evidence: Trajectory groups can only be assigned to individuals with a complete exposure window, so people who die or are lost mid-window are handled by a weight and by an assumption that missingness in the trajectory is at random conditional on the groups. The process generating incomplete exposure follow-up is treated as something to reweight and impute rather than as a structure that determines which trajectories are observable at all.
problems.quote: Another limitation is that the LCGA step assumes that missingness in the treatment trajectory is MAR conditional on the groups.

papers.title: A MARGINAL STRUCTURAL MODEL FOR PARTIAL COMPLIANCE IN SMARTS.
papers.one_line: A marginal structural model with principal stratification on continuous compliance in a 159-patient sequential multiple assignment randomized trial shows the optimal embedded regime changes with compliance stratum, reversing the ranking obtained under intention to treat.
papers.what_was_done: Mean outcomes under embedded dynamic treatment regimes were defined as functions of continuous potential compliance rather than binary complier status, and estimated with a marginal structural model whose latent potential compliances are imputed by a Dirichlet process mixture with data augmentation. Simulations used correlated truncated normal and correlated Beta compliance margins; bias fell with sample size, for example from 0.04 to 0.03 for the stage-1 treatment by compliance interaction against a true value of -0.8, and median joint Bayesian coverage for multiple comparisons with the best was 95.04 percent with multiplicity adjustment against 87.89 percent without. The application was the ENGAGE trial of alcohol and cocaine dependence, in which patients who failed to engage in intensive outpatient programming after two weeks were randomized to two motivational interviewing interventions and rerandomized at week eight, with noncompliance rates at or above 50 percent and a total sample of n = 159, split into subgroups of n = 88 and n = 71 by median treatment readiness. Fitted models gave, for the first stage assignment, an intercept of 3.12 with coefficients -1.59 and -0.23 on stage-1 potential compliances and 6.53 on the stage-2 treatment by compliance interaction. Under intention to treat the regimes beginning with intensive outpatient programming dominated, but at specific compliance strata the patient choice regimes entered the set of best. The compliance range observed in the trial is acknowledged to differ from clinical practice, in which case the method extrapolates.

future_research.gap: Extension to observational data and to zero-inflated compliance is not done
future_research.quote: Although beyond the scope of this paper, future work should extend the methodology to observational data and also account for zero-inflation, which would be particularly useful

future_research.gap: Measurement error in the outcome interacts with compliance adjustment in unknown ways
future_research.quote: Hence, it is of interest to account measurement error in the outcome and study its effect when adjusting for compliance.

future_research.gap: Model selection for marginal structural models is unresolved
future_research.quote: Model selection in MSMs is an important topic that merits further research.

problems.evidence: Compliance is treated as a continuous quantity, the fraction of sessions attended, and the stated reason is that the cut point separating compliers from noncompliers cannot be chosen defensibly. That replaces an arbitrary equivalence class with a continuum and shows the ranking of regimes changes across it. It does not close the problem: the strata are latent, must be imputed from a Dirichlet process mixture, and no clinical criterion establishes which compliance levels constitute the same treatment.
problems.quote: Adjusting for partial as opposed to binary compliance allows for more flexibility when there is continuous compliance and the threshold for compliers versus noncompliers is not easily chosen.

problems.evidence: The estimand is indexed by compliance stratum, and compliance in a trial that recruits and monitors patients is higher than in routine care. Carrying the estimate to a practice setting therefore requires evaluating the model outside the compliance range observed in the 159 trial patients, which is stated plainly to be extrapolation, with no accounting attached to it.
problems.quote: Note that in the case that the compliance range in a SMART is different from the real world setting, the method is extrapolating.

problems.evidence: Potential compliance under the regime a patient did not receive is unobservable, so the target quantity becomes a mean outcome within latent principal strata whose membership is imputed rather than measured. That is a different estimand from the mean under an assigned regime, and it is named as such and modeled explicitly. What remains open is that the resulting quantity is defined by the imputation model: a different mixture specification defines different strata and therefore a different target.
problems.quote: An important challenge with principal stratification is that some of the potential compliances are latent.

problems.evidence: The intention to treat contrast averages over patients with different compliance levels, and its magnitude is stated to shrink as noncompliance grows, in a trial where noncompliance exceeds 50 percent. The same mechanism operates in an observational emulation whose arms converge, and the fix demonstrated here requires modeling compliance as a continuous latent variable rather than reporting the attenuated contrast.
problems.quote: In fact, the ITT effect estimate will likely diminish as noncompliance increases

problems.evidence: The subgroup analysis split 159 patients at the median treatment readiness into groups of 88 and 71, and in one of them every embedded regime remained in the set of best. Membership in that set is explicitly not equivalence; it reflects intervals too wide to exclude clinically inferior regimes, so the subgroups with the least information return the least discriminating answers.
problems.quote: Specifically, low power makes it challenging to rule out inferior EDTRs.

problems.evidence: The full trial contributes 159 patients, but the parameters that distinguish stage-2 regimes are identified only from nonresponders, and as the engagement rate rises that subsample shrinks and the stage-2 standard errors grow while bias is unaffected. The quantity that limits inference is the number of patients on the relevant treatment sequence, not the enrolled total.
problems.quote: This would shrink the treatment sequence sample size for nonresponders.
